chapter: Art Tatum, Parker and chord thinking
title: Closing eyes versus contacting the audience, Daniel and the lions
summary: He explains why his wife made him open his eyes on stage, and the power of the eyes over audiences.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah, because you do the same thing.
Because you’re so into the spirit of the song. You’re out of this world, is what it really is. You’re not in this world.
And I find that I focus better with my eyes closed.
Absolutely, because music is spiritual, so you don’t need your eyes.
I really want to be one with the music, and hopefully the audience gets it.

Exactly, but you need to contact the audience with your eyes. Your eyes have a magnetism to them. A man has dominion over all the animals because of his eyes. A man can, through his eyes and the sound of his voice, tame any animal. A man should fear no animal. This is a natural fact. This is the story of Daniel in the lion’s den. Daniel had the gift of dream interpretation and dominion over animals. The lions came. Daniel looked at them and spoke to them, and they lay down. That’s why it’s necessary, like they teach you in acting, to focus. You focus your eyes on your fellow actor. You make focused gestures. James Cagney was very famous for this. He would deliver a line and he would use his hands. He would say, “I’m not going to give nothing. I’m giving you nothing.” But he’s also pointing to you, to say, you got the next line. Now deliver it back to me. He was a great help to other actors because of things like that. They call them focused gestures.
